summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Praxis Health through the model catalog UI, discussed open-model selection (LLama variants, Mistral, Mosaic), benchmark methodology, and compatibility matrices for hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Customer asked about latency vs cost tradeoffs, KV cache and quantization support, and SOC2/KMS integrations. Agreed next steps: run a short benchmark on Praxis's de-identified data, share compatibility matrix and pricing, and schedule a technical check-in to validate VPC access.
transcript:
[00:00] Alice (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Alice Monroe, AE at Redwood. With me is Ben Cho, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya (Praxis): Good, thanks. Maya here. We've been looking forward to seeing the model catalog demo and understanding how we can pick an open model for clinical note summarization.
[00:16] Tom (CTO): Hi, Tom. Main things for us are latency under 300ms for short completions, cost per 1k tokens, and of course security - SOC2 and KMS.
[00:28] Ben (Redwood SE): Great, we'll walk through the console, the model catalog, benchmarking results, and the compatibility matrix for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Quick note, I'm going to share my screen.
[00:38] Alice: If you see references to our "Model Cat" or "model catalog", that's the UI tab we'll demo.
[00:46] [Screen share starts]
[01:02] Ben: Okay so first slide — the catalog lists curated open models. We include performance profiles: latency percentiles, token throughput, memory footprint, and optimal quantization formats. Example entries: Llama-3-13B (int8/llm-q8), Mistral 7B-v1, Mosaic 14B.
[01:20] Maya: Quick question — do you actually host these models or are they pointers to customers' self-hosted endpoints?
[01:27] Ben: Good question. For hosted API we run the model variants in our runtime. For Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools, and Private gives you a control plane with an on-prem or VPC runtime. The compatibility matrix on the right shows which models are supported in each mode.
[01:40] Tom: And the matrix also shows quantization support?
[01:44] Ben: Yep, we annotate whether a model can be run int8, q4_0, q5_k etc, and whether KV cache savings are available.
[01:52] [01:52] Sofia (Infra): We need to know whether the runtime supports progressive batching and prefetching for short chat requests; we have many small requests across clinics.
[02:03] Ben: Absolutely — our serving runtime supports continuous batching and adaptive batching heuristics. For chat-like workloads the KV cache is used to avoid recomputation for prefixes, which lowers p99 tail latency.
[02:13] Maya: There's been chatter about "Redwood Optimize" doing automatic batching and cache suggestions; can you show that?
[02:19] Ben: Sure — in the Optimize tab we surface recommendations: batch size targets, suggested quantization profile, and estimated cost savings. Quick caveat: those estimates are heuristic unless you run a benchmark with your actual sequence length distribution.
[02:33] Ben: Let me jump to a benchmark we ran for a healthcare summarization workload (synthetic) — this is 1k short documents, average input 220 tokens, outputs around 80 tokens. For Llama-3-13B int8 on a p4-like instance we hit median latency ~210ms, 95th ~420ms, and cost roughly $0.09 per 1k tokens.
[02:53] Tom: Those 95th percentiles are concerning. How do you get them down?
[02:57] Ben: A few levers — dedicated reserved capacity (no cold start variability), intelligent routing to a lower-latency region, smaller model family for short tasks (e.g., Mistral 7B with good fine-tune), or more aggressive quantization. Also prefix caching helps a lot for repeated prompts.
[03:14] [03:14] Maya: On the fine-tune note — how do we evaluate quality tradeoffs? We can't sacrifice clinical accuracy for cost.
[03:21] Ben: Great point. We recommend an eval corpus and quality metrics pipeline. In the catalog each model card links to evaluation runs we did on public benchmarks and you can plug in your own eval set to compare Rouge/BLEU/clinical-precision. We'll run a small A/B compare as part of the POC.
[03:36] Tom: If we run in our VPC, is the KV cache stored only in customer infra? How do you handle encryption?
[03:43] Ben: In Private deployments the KV cache and the runtime memory live entirely in your environment. We support KMS integrations for model encryption and key rotation. For Dedicated / Hosted we use envelope encryption and can integrate with customer-managed keys for certain enterprise plans.
[03:58] Sofia: Does the console show real-time token-level cost breakdowns?
[04:02] Alice: Yep, the Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model. You can also set per-model quotas and autoscaling policies.
[04:12] [04:12] Maya: Back to model selection — what are your recommended open models for clinical summarization where hallucination risk must be low?
[04:19] Ben: We usually start with mid-sized instruction-tuned open models (7B-13B) that have been fine-tuned on question/answer and summarization tasks. We also surface models that were trained with biomedical corpora. For lower hallucination we prioritize models with recent RL or instruction tuning and then run targeted evals.
[04:36] Tom: Do you provide model lineage and provenance metadata in the catalog? We need to audit training data sources for compliance.
[04:42] Ben: We include model provenance fields where available (source repo, upstream license, known training corpora). For enterprise customers we can provide more detailed attestations as part of the compliance package.
[04:54] [05:00] Alice: I'm going to show the compatibility matrix now — this is a downloadable CSV and also surfaced inline. It maps model -> hosted/dedicated/private -> quantization formats -> recommended GPU type -> notes.
[05:13] Maya: Can you share that matrix after the call?
[05:16] Alice: Absolutely, will include in the follow-up.
[05:20] [05:20] Ben: Now a quick note about benchmarking methodology: we run realistic load profiles, 95/99 tail capture, synthetic user traces, and we can also run a customer-provided sample in a short pre-flight benchmark. Results in the catalog are normalized to a per-token basis and a hardware spec.
[05:36] Tom: For a POC, we'd want a 1-hour run with our de-identified sample and the option to run in our VPC. How invasive is that?
[05:45] Ben: Not invasive — we can run a remote benchmark against a small VPC enclave or you can provide pre-signed S3 with the sample. For private deployments we can also run the benchmark inside your environment.
[05:55] Sofia: Network egress is a concern for us. If you benchmark hosted from your cloud region, will data leave our VPC?
[06:02] Ben: For hosted, data flows through our managed endpoints. If you need to ensure data doesn't leave your VPC, we'll do a Private deployment or run the benchmark inside your network.
[06:10] Maya: What about model updates and rollouts? We need predictable versioning for clinical models.
[06:15] Ben: The Console has rollout controls: pin model versions to routes, canary deploys, A/B tests, automatic fallbacks, and audit logs. You can set a policy to prevent auto-upgrades.
[06:26] [06:30] Alice: Let's go through a short demo of the model card for "Mistral-7B-clinical-v1" — you can see the eval tab, latency numbers, quant options, and a note that it's supported in Hosted and Dedicated, but for Private it's supported with q8 formats only due to kernel constraints.
[06:45] Tom: Kernel constraints?
[06:47] Ben: Some quant kernels we use in the Hosted runtime rely on proprietary acceleration; in Private deployments we provide compatible open kernels but not all combinations are available initially. It's in the compatibility notes.
[06:58] Maya: That's fine, we can take the models that are supported in our mode.
[07:02] [07:02] Ben: One minor transcription artifact you might see in auto-exports is model names reversed — occasionally the pipeline outputs "Mistral Llama" — ignore that, it's a known NER in the exporter.
[07:15] [07:15] Tom: Let's talk numbers — what's the cost diff between Hosted and Dedicated for our workload?
[07:19] Alice: Hosted is fully usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity so you get better unit economics at volume. For your estimated 2M tokens/day, Dedicated tends to be X% cheaper depending on GPU selection and utilization. We'll send a modeled cost sheet.
[07:34] Tom: Are there any plug-and-play model families that you recommend for clinical summarization?
[07:39] Ben: Mistral 7B variants and Llama-3-13B tuned on medical corpora are good starting points. Also check Mosaic-14B if you need longer context. But Mistral tends to have strong instruction-following for summary tasks.
[07:51] Maya: Do you support function calling and structured output so we can get JSON with fields like diagnosis, medication list?
[07:58] Ben: Yes, the API supports function/tool calling and structured output. We also have schema validation hooks in the Console that flag outputs outside expected ranges.
[08:08] [08:08] Sofia: We're curious about quantization-induced regression — do you run quality checks post-quant?
[08:13] Ben: Yes, Optimize recommends a quant profile and flags if eval metrics drop beyond thresholds; you can configure rollback policies. But we always recommend validating with your clinical eval set before wide rollout.
[08:25] Maya: On that validation, what is your recommended sample size for a robust comparison?
[08:29] Ben: For initial POC, 500-1,000 annotated examples gives good signal; for production-grade confidence you want several thousand with stratified cases.
[08:40] [08:40] Alice: Quick poll — is the team leaning toward Hosted POC with a plan to re-evaluate Dedicated, or planning Private from the start?
[08:48] Tom: We prefer to start hosted for speed but we might require Private long-term for compliance.
[08:52] Maya: Agreed, start hosted POC but we need to validate egress and encryption.
[08:58] Ben: Sounds good. We'll run the POC in Hosted first, then test transition steps to Dedicated or Private.
[09:05] [09:05] Ben: I'm going to switch to the Console to demo the Optimize suggestions — here you can input your token distribution and we output batch and cache recommendations plus expected cost delta.
[09:18] Alice: Note that Optimize's numbers are estimates until you run a customer-provided benchmark.
[09:24] Maya: We'll definitely want the benchmark. What telemetry do you need from us?
[09:29] Ben: Either a representative sample file or an API trace with sequence lengths and payloads. For VPC benchmarking, credentials to a temporary enclave or pre-signed S3 sample works.
[09:38] Sofia: We'll need an internal ticket to produce that sample; what's the minimum data sanitization you need?
[09:43] Ben: De-identification is fine; we don't need PHI for a runtime benchmark. Clinical structure preserved (sections, entity tokens) is helpful.
[09:53] Tom: On the security front, share your SOC2 report and details on KMS integration.
[09:58] Alice: We'll include SOC2 docs and a KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
[10:03] [10:03] Maya: Any references to competitors you want to call out? We evaluated Anthropic and OpenAI last quarter.
[10:09] Ben: Many teams compare us on price/perf vs OpenAI and on self-host flexibility vs Anthropic/Replicate. Our differentiator is the unified runtime and cost controls for inference.
[10:20] [10:20] Tom: Let's talk timeline — if we start a POC next week, how fast can we get benchmarks back?
[10:25] Ben: If you provide the sample this week we can run a 1-hour benchmark and have results within 48 hours.
[10:31] Alice: We'll also share the model catalog PDF and the compatibility matrix CSV after the call.
[10:38] [10:38] Maya: Great. One more technical — do you support context windows beyond 16k? We have some long-case histories.
[10:45] Ben: We support models up to 32k and with window management for very long contexts. For large-context tasks we recommend Mosaic-14B-32k or customized context-split strategies.
[10:56] [11:00] Tom: Any special requirements for running the POC in our VPC? We want minimal changes to our network.
[11:07] Ben: For an in-VPC POC we typically require a small test subnet, optional NAT or VPC peering, and IAM role for temporary S3 access. We'll provide Terraform snippets.
[11:19] Sofia: Terraform snippets would be ideal.
[11:22] Alice: We'll add those to the follow-up.
[11:26] [11:26] Ben: Also nutty thing — you'll see small transcript artifacts from Fireflies when we export; ignore the odd punctuation and some entity swaps.
[11:36] [11:36] Maya: On SLA — what are your uptime and latency SLOs for Dedicated?
[11:40] Alice: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets — we can share the SLA document.
[11:46] Tom: Good. Let's capture next steps.
[11:50] Alice: Recap: 1) Ben to run benchmark with Praxis sample (or we run hosted with de-id sample) 2) Alice to send model catalog + compatibility matrix + pricing + SOC2 docs 3) Sofia to share minimal VPC test access or pre-signed sample. Agreed?
[12:09] Maya: Agreed.
[12:12] Tom: Agreed.
[12:14] Alice: Perfect. We'll schedule a technical check-in after the benchmark.
[12:18] [12:18] Ben: I'll open a JIRA/Slack thread for the benchmark coordination.
[12:23] Maya: Thanks, everyone.
[12:25] Alice: Thanks, team. We'll follow up by end of day tomorrow with the docs.
[12:30] [12:30] Call ends.

Note: occasional transcription errors and name misspellings in auto-export (e.g., "Model Cat" instead of "Model Catalog"). Links shared during call: model-catalog PDF (link: https://redwood.example.com/model-catalog.pdf), compatibility matrix CSV (link: https://redwood.example.com/compatibility-matrix-praxis.csv), benchmark notebook (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/praxis-2026-06).
